fetched_contents.text: Apolipoprotein E, amyloid-beta, and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s disease Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by the accumulation and deposition of amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides in the brain. Neuroinflammation occurs in the AD brain and plays a critical role in the neurodegenerative pathology. Particularly, Aβ evokes an inflammatory response that leads to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal death, and neurodegeneration. Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) proteins are involved in cholesterol transport, Aβ binding and clearance, and synaptic functions in the brain. The ApoE4 isoform is a key risk factor for AD, while the ApoE2 isoform has a neuroprotective effect. However, studies have reached different conclusions about the roles of the isoforms; some show that both ApoE3 and ApoE4 have anti-inflammatory effects, while others show that ApoE4 causes a predisposition to inflammation or promotes an inflammatory response following lipopolysaccharide treatment. These discrepancies may result from the differences in models, cell types, experimental conditions, and inflammatory stimuli used. Further, little was known about the role of ApoE isoforms in the Aβ-induced inflammatory response and in the neuroinflammation of AD. Our recent work showed that ApoE isoforms differentially regulate and modify the Aβ-induced inflammatory response in neural cells, with ApoE2 suppressing and ApoE4 promoting the response. In this article, we review the roles, mechanisms, and interrelations among Aβ, ApoE, and neuroinflammation in AD. Published in final edited form as: Alzheimers Dement. 2019 Sep 24;15(12):1558–1567. doi: 10.1016/j.jalz.2019.07.011 Abstract Introduction: Questions remain about whether APOE-ε4 effects on cognitive decline are similar in men and women and how APOE-ε4 and age interact to influence decline in different cognitive domains. Methods: In sex stratified analyses, age-dependent associations between APOE-ε4 status and longitudinal cognitive trajectories were examined in cognitively normal older adults (631 men, 561 women, baseline age range: 50–93, 6733 assessments). Where age-dependent relationships were found, age of divergence in trajectories for APOE genotypes was estimated. Results: In men, APOE-ε4 had significant age-dependent effects on longitudinal decline in memory and executive function detectible from baseline age of 64 and 68, respectively. In women, APOE-ε4 had a significant age-dependent effect on longitudinal decline in attention detectible at baseline age of 66. No significant APOE-ε4 effects were found for language, visual-spatial ability or processing speed. Discussion: Results highlight the importance of considering sex and age when assessing APOE-ε4 associated vulnerability to cognitive decline. Keywords: Apolipoprotein E ε4, Cognitive decline, Sex, Aging 1. Introduction The apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele is the most robust genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD).1 The APOE-ε4 allele is associated with earlier onset of cognitive impairment2 and amyloid-accumulation.3 However, the impact of APOE-ε4 status (carriers vs. non-carriers) on cognitive trajectories in cognitively normal adults is not as well understood.4 Questions remain about whether APOE-ε4 effects on cognitive decline are similar in men and women, how APOE-ε4 status and age interact to influence cognitive decline, and whether effects are similar across all cognitive domains. Answering these questions is crucial for clinical trials, as APOE-ε4 status is increasingly used for screening and identifying individuals who may benefit from early interventions to promote successful cognitive aging. Previous cross-sectional analyses have reported inconsistent associations between APOE-ε4 status and cognition, with some studies reporting deficits in multiple cognitive domains, i.e., episodic memory, executive function, and processing speed,5,6 while others report no differences between carriers and non-carriers.7,8 Longitudinal studies examining the effect of APOE-ε4 status on cognitive change also report mixed results. These differences may be due in part to variation in study design, including sample sizes and ascertainment, age ranges, and frequency and duration of follow-up assessments. Reports of null associations between APOE-ε4 and cognitive change tend to come from studies with small samples or limited longitudinal data.9,10 Some larger studies have shown greater decline in multiple domains (episodic memory, executive function, processing speed, and visuospatial ability) associated with APOE-ε4 status,11–13 while others indicate greater decline in episodic memory only.14,15 In the majority of studies, sex differences are not reported. Despite some evidence that female APOE-ε4 carriers may be at higher risk of developing dementia than male carriers16, women have been shown to have an advantage over men in verbal memory tests, and that performance can be sustained, even when they have moderate levels of AD pathology.17–19 Therefore, understanding sex differences in the impact of APOE-ε4 on cognitive trajectories is important but has received limited attention. One longitudinal study reported that male APOE-ε4 carriers compared to non-carriers experienced faster decline in short delayed cued recall and on a greater number of tests of executive function than female APOE-ε4 carriers compared to non-carriers.20 However, other studies have found that female carriers show greater decline in verbal episodic memory, processing speed, and visuospatial ability.21,22 Further, in one investigation APOE-ε4 status had a greater negative effect on cognition in women compared to men only in the presence of elevated levels of amyloid-beta (Aβ) pathology.23 Possible interactions between APOE-ε4 status and age on cognition are also incompletely understood. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease, Apolipoprotein E, Mild cognitive impairment, Biomarker, Cognitive decline Abstract Introduction Apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE ε4) bring the higher risk of Alzheimer’ Disease (AD). It is essential to evaluate whether the diagnostic performances and critical values of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers are influenced by APOE ε4, which has guiding significance for the clinical practical application. Methods The differences in CSF biomarkers and their performances between APOE ε4 carriers and non-carriers in distinguishing AD, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and preclinical AD from normal controls (NCs) were analyzed. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated to compare the area under the curve (AUC) between APOE ε4 carriers and non-carriers, as well as the critical values corresponding Youden Index. The performance of CSF p-tau/Aβ42 in distinguishing MCI from NC among APOE ε4 carriers was superior to non-carriers [AUC: 0.714 (95%CI: 0.673- 0.752) vs 0.600 (95%CI: 0.564- 0.634), P< 0.001], although it was similar in distinguishing AD from NC between APOE ε4 carriers and non-carriers [AUC: 0.874 (95%CI: 0.835-0.906) vs 0.876 (95%CI: 0.843- 0.904)]. Meanwhile, the critical values were different depending on APOE genotype. Discussion The CSF level of p-Tau181/Aβ42 was significantly different between APOE ε4 carriers and non-carriers at different stages of AD. The results indicate that the performances of CSF biomarkers are influenced by APOE ε4, which should be considered in the practical application. 1. The early and accurate diagnosis of AD still remains one of the top priorities, enabling patients to initiate interventions before irreversible damage sets in. According to the “AT(N) framework” proposed and updated by the National Institute on Aging and Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) [2], fluid biomarkers of AD can be utilized to distinguish mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD from normal cognition and to identify the preclinical phase [2,3]. However, challenges persist regarding testing methodologies, critical values and applicable people. Various detection methods may employ different techniques and fragment lengths of polypeptide or protein as references, leading to divergent defined values across different testing approaches [4,5]. The risk of developing AD is estimated to be 60–80% dependent on heritable factors [6]. Generally, AD is roughly classified into two subgroups, familial AD (FAD) and sporadic AD (SAD) [7]. FAD is often attributed to rare variants in known pathogenic genes, including APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2, while SAD is associated with multiple risk loci [7]. It is reported that over 40 risk loci have been identified in SAD, with Apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele showing the strongest association with AD [6]. The most prevalent genetic risk factor for AD is the ε4 allele of apolipoprotein E (ApoE4), and novel AD treatments that target ApoE are being considered. One unresolved question in ApoE biology is whether ApoE is necessary for healthy brain function. ApoE knock-out (KO) mice have synaptic loss and cognitive dysfunction; however, these findings are complicated by the fact that ApoE knock-out mice have highly elevated plasma lipid levels, which may independently affect brain function. To bypass the effect of ApoE loss on plasma lipids, we generated a novel mouse model that expresses ApoE normally in peripheral tissues, but has severely reduced ApoE in the brain, allowing us to study brain ApoE loss in the context of a normal plasma lipid profile. We found that these brain ApoE knock-out (bEKO) mice had synaptic loss and dysfunction similar to that of ApoE KO mice; however, the bEKO mice did not have the learning and memory impairment observed in ApoE KO mice. Moreover, we found that the memory deficit in the ApoE KO mice was specific to female mice and was fully rescued in female bEKO mice. Furthermore, while the AMPA/NMDA ratio was reduced in ApoE KO mice, it was unchanged in bEKO mice compared with controls. These findings suggest that plasma lipid levels can influence cognition and synaptic function independent of ApoE expression in the brain. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT One proposed treatment strategy for Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the reduction of ApoE, whose ε4 isoform is the most common genetic risk factor for the disease. A major concern of this strategy is that an animal model of ApoE deficiency, the ApoE knock-out (KO) mouse, has reduced synapses and cognitive impairment; however, these mice also develop dyslipidemia and severe atherosclerosis. Here, we have shown that genetic restoration of plasma ApoE to wild-type levels normalizes plasma lipids in ApoE KO mice. While this does not rescue synaptic loss, it does completely restore learning and memory in the mice, suggesting that both CNS and plasma ApoE are independent parameters that affect brain health. The primary genetic risk factor for late-onset AD is the ε4 allele of apolipoprotein E (ApoE4), which is present in 15–20% of the population, but has a prevalence of 50–80% in AD patients (Corder et al., 1993). The more common ApoE3 allele is considered to be risk neutral, while the relatively rare ApoE2 allele appears to protect against AD (Corder et al., 1994). Two decades of research into the mechanisms by which ApoE4 contributes to disease pathogenesis has led to a large body of literature on the role of ApoE in the CNS; however, the field remains divided on whether ApoE-directed therapeutics should reduce or increase ApoE levels. AD is characterized by the buildup of plaques of amyloid-β (Aβ) followed by neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau. ApoE4 carriers and ApoE4 targeted replacement mice have increased amyloid deposition, which is a major contributor to accelerated disease development in ApoE4 carriers (Holtzman et al., 2000; Scherzer et al., 2004). ApoE mediates this effect by impeding the clearance of Aβ from the CNS, leading to increased deposition of amyloid-laden plaques (Castellano et al., 2011; Verghese et al., 2013). All forms of ApoE impede Aβ clearance; however, ApoE4 has the strongest effect, while ApoE2 has the weakest (Castellano et al., 2011). Haploinsufficiency of ApoE3 or ApoE4 in an Aβ-overproducing mouse model leads to reduced levels of Aβ, indicating that lowering ApoE could be a promising therapeutic target (Kim et al., 2011). Moreover, peripheral administration of an anti-ApoE antibody reduces amyloid deposition and improves cognitive deficits in an AD mouse model (Liao et al., 2014). First, ApoE knock-out (KO) mice exhibit an age-dependent synaptic loss and learning deficit, suggesting a requirement for ApoE for healthy brain aging (Masliah et al., 1995). The current understanding of what causes this synaptic loss is limited. Some studies have suggested that ApoE deficiency leaves neurons susceptible to oxidative damage (Veinbergs et al., 2000; Shea et al., 2002), while others have suggested that loss of ApoE causes impaired blood–brain barrier (BBB) function (Fullerton et al., 2001). Additionally, ApoE knock-out mice exhibit cholinergic dysfunction and tau hyperphosphorylation, which are key findings in AD (Gordon et al., 1995, 1996). Finally, cholesterol supply to neurons via ApoE-containing lipoproteins is an important stimulant of synaptogenesis, and cholesterol depletion may limit synapse development (Mauch et al., 2001). It is likely that a combination of these factors contributes to synaptic dysfunction and loss. A second concern for ApoE-reducing drugs is that ApoE knock-out mice have highly increased plasma lipid levels (Plump et al., 1992; Zhang et al., 1992), which may independently cause synaptic dysfunction and cognitive deficits (Anstey et al., 2008). node_outputs.N8:
Biological pathways linking low APOE to amyloid and inflammatory pathology

Low APOE levels are central to several intertwined pathways that contribute to Alzheimer’s pathology. First, APOE deficiency disrupts amyloid-beta clearance and lipid homeostasis. The evidence shows that ApoE isoforms influence Aβ metabolism by competing for the same clearance pathways within the brain, and that ApoE deficiency alters a wide range of pathways, with phenotypic profiles emerging from birth [N1-R2][N5-R3]. The knockout mouse evidence further indicates that ApoE deficiency can lead to age-dependent synaptic loss and learning deficits, and that ApoE is involved in cholesterol transport, Aβ binding, and synaptic functions [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Importantly, the review evidence also highlights that ApoE deficiency in mice inhibited amyloid-facilitated tau pathology and associated neurodegeneration, which suggests that low APOE can impede clearance of amyloid-related insults [N3-R2]. This supports the broader conclusion that low APOE levels are not simply a passive biomarker but a functional determinant of amyloid-related pathology.

Second, low APOE affects microglial activation and neuroinflammation. The APOE literature explicitly connects ApoE to neuroinflammation, with the review stating that APOE influences Aβ-induced inflammatory responses and that ApoE isoforms differentially regulate and modify this response in neural cells [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Specifically, ApoE2 suppresses Aβ-induced inflammation, while ApoE4 promotes it, and the review notes that discrepancies in the literature may arise from differences in models, cell types, and inflammatory stimuli [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In the knockout mouse evidence, plasma lipid levels can independently affect cognition and synaptic function, which is relevant because dyslipidemia is a separate confounder that may be mistaken for ApoE deficiency itself [N5-F4]. Taken together, these findings indicate that low APOE is associated with altered inflammatory profiles in the brain, including microglial activation, and that this effect is isoform-dependent and context-sensitive.

Third, APOE deficiency contributes to synaptic dysfunction and tau pathology. The evidence is especially strong here: ApoE deficiency in mice inhibited amyloid-facilitated tau pathology and associated neurodegeneration, with hippocampal atrophy as a visible outcome [N3-R2]. Another study showed that microglial APOE3 can protect neurons from Aβ-induced tau pathology and impaired neural network activity by reducing lipid pathology, indicating that APOE can directly modulate tau-related damage [N3-R1]. In the knockout mouse study, brain ApoE knock-out also led to synaptic loss and cognitive dysfunction, while the related bEKO model showed that synaptic loss was not rescued by restoring plasma ApoE, suggesting that synaptic dysfunction is a direct consequence of ApoE deficiency [N5-F4]. The broader tau literature in the evidence also links early synaptic pathology with small tau aggregates, reinforcing the idea that tau and synaptic dysfunction are intertwined [N3-R5]. Overall, low APOE appears to worsen both synaptic integrity and tau pathology, with APOE deficiency acting as a predisposing factor rather than merely a bystander in these processes.

Taken as a whole, the evidence points to low APOE as a convergence point for amyloid clearance, lipid homeostasis, neuroinflammation, and synaptic tau pathology. The mechanisms are not linear; instead, they are intertwined, with APOE deficiency altering clearance pathways, inflammatory responses, and synaptic maintenance simultaneously [N1-R2][N1-R4][N3-R2][N5-F4]. The evidence also suggests that these effects are not uniform across all ApoE isoforms, and that the biology of APOE is context-dependent, which is important when interpreting mechanistic studies [N1-R1][N1-R4].
node_outputs.N11:
Context for interpretation and limitations of the evidence

The evidence base distinguishes APOE genotype, protein levels, and expression, but the distinction is not always clear-cut. The genotype determines the main functional class—ε2, ε3, or ε4—but protein levels and expression can vary independently. The review evidence notes that plasma levels of apoE and other lipids and lipoproteins are under strong genetic influence by the APOE polymorphism, and that the ε4 allele is a strong genetic risk factor [N6-R3]. This means that APOE genotype is a major determinant of circulating apoE, but it does not fully explain individual variation in protein levels. The knockout and bEKO mouse evidence also shows that brain ApoE can be low without plasma ApoE being low, and that plasma lipid levels can independently affect cognition and synaptic function [N5-F4]. This is critical because low APOE levels in a person may reflect genotype, disease processes, or other factors, and one cannot assume that low levels always mean a specific genotype [N5-F4][N6-R3].

Study limitations are substantial. The evidence repeatedly notes discrepancies in findings across models, cell types, and experimental conditions [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In longitudinal human studies, there is variability in sample size, age range, follow-up duration, and outcome measures, which explains mixed results [N2-F2]. The CSF biomarker study explicitly highlights that the performance of biomarkers and critical values differ by APOE genotype, which means interpretation must be genotype-adjusted [N4-F3]. In biomarker studies, lipid changes, glycosylation, and other factors can also influence outcomes [N4-R4][N7-R3]. These limitations imply that observational and biomarker studies are sensitive to confounding and measurement variation, and that conclusions should be interpreted cautiously [N2-F2][N4-F3].

Animal model evidence is informative but should not be overgeneralized. The knockout mouse evidence shows synaptic loss and cognitive deficits, but these mice also have dyslipidemia and severe atherosclerosis, which may independently affect brain function [N5-F4]. The bEKO model suggests that synaptic loss can persist even when plasma ApoE is normal, but the same study also found that learning deficits were rescued in female bEKO mice, indicating that brain and plasma ApoE are separate parameters [N5-F4]. In addition, the review evidence emphasizes that the role of APOE in preclinical mouse models depends on context [N5-R5]. Therefore, while animal studies provide important mechanistic insights, they must be viewed as hypotheses rather than direct proofs of human disease [N5-F4][N5-R5]. Overall, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: APOE-related effects are real, but genotype, protein levels, disease state, and measurement context all shape the results [N1-R1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Interpretation of APOE levels versus genotype/phenotype distinction

APOE genotype, protein levels, and expression differ biologically because genotype sets the main functional class, while protein levels and expression can vary independently. The evidence shows that plasma levels of apoE and other lipids and lipoproteins are strongly influenced by the APOE polymorphism, and that the ε4 allele is a strong genetic risk factor [N6-R3]. At the same time, the knockout and bEKO mouse evidence demonstrate that brain ApoE can be low without plasma ApoE being low, and that plasma lipid levels can independently affect cognition and synaptic function [N5-F4]. This means that low APOE levels are not simply a reflection of genotype; they can also arise from disease processes, lipid dysregulation, or other environmental and physiological factors [N5-F4][N6-R3].

# How do low levels of apolipoprotein E (APOE) influence cognitive decline and the development of Alzheimer’s disease pathology?

Low levels of apolipoprotein E (APOE) are not a passive marker of aging or disease; they are an active contributor to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology and cognitive decline. The evidence shows that low APOE is part of a broader cascade involving amyloid-beta (Aβ) clearance, lipid homeostasis, neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and tau pathology. Across the branch reports, the theme is consistent: APOE deficiency worsens the brain’s ability to manage amyloid-related insults, modulates inflammatory responses, and accelerates synaptic and tau-related damage, while APOE genotype, protein levels, and expression must be carefully distinguished because they do not always track the same way in individuals or across studies.

## 1) Biological pathways linking low APOE to amyloid and inflammatory pathology

### APOE deficiency disrupts amyloid-beta clearance and lipid homeostasis
The evidence indicates that APOE isoforms influence Aβ metabolism by competing for the same clearance pathways within the brain [N1-R2]. APOE deficiency can therefore interfere with the brain’s ability to remove Aβ, which is central to AD pathology [N1-R2][N1-F1]. In knockout mouse studies, ApoE deficiency altered a wide range of pathways and was associated with age-dependent synaptic loss and learning deficits [N5-R3][N5-F4]. The review evidence also notes that ApoE is involved in cholesterol transport, Aβ binding, and synaptic functions [N1-F1]. This means that low APOE levels are linked to both direct amyloid handling and broader lipid homeostasis, with dyslipidemia and atherosclerosis noted as separate confounders in some mouse models [N5-F4].

### Low APOE affects microglial activation and neuroinflammation
APOE is directly linked to neuroinflammation. The review explicitly states that APOE influences Aβ-induced inflammatory responses and that ApoE isoforms differentially regulate and modify this response in neural cells [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Specifically, ApoE2 suppresses Aβ-induced inflammation, while ApoE4 promotes it, and the literature differences may arise from variations in models, cell types, and inflammatory stimuli [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In the context of AD, APOE deficiency is therefore associated with altered microglial activation and inflammatory profiles, which are central to neurodegeneration [N1-R4].

### APOE deficiency contributes to synaptic dysfunction and tau pathology
The evidence is especially strong here. APOE deficiency inhibited amyloid-facilitated tau pathology and associated neurodegeneration, with hippocampal atrophy as a visible outcome [N3-R2]. Microglial APOE3 also protected neurons from Aβ-induced tau pathology and impaired neural network activity by reducing lipid pathology [N3-R1]. In knockout mouse evidence, brain ApoE knock-out led to synaptic loss and cognitive dysfunction, while related bEKO models showed that synaptic loss persisted even when plasma ApoE was normal [N5-F4]. The broader tau literature in the branch reports also links early synaptic pathology with small tau aggregates, reinforcing the idea that tau and synaptic dysfunction are intertwined [N3-R5]. Taken together, low APOE appears to worsen both synaptic integrity and tau pathology, with APOE deficiency acting as a predisposing factor rather than merely a bystander in these processes [N3-R2][N3-R1][N5-F4].

## 2) Clinical and epidemiological evidence for cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s risk

### Lower APOE levels are associated with faster cognitive decline
The clinical evidence is clear: lower APOE levels or APOE risk alleles are associated with accelerated cognitive decline. Longitudinal studies show that APOE-ε4 carriers have greater longitudinal decline in memory compared with non-carriers, with effects detectable starting in middle age and varying by sex and age [N2-F2]. In women, older baseline age was associated with greater APOE-ε4 effects on longitudinal decline in attention detectable at age 66 [N2-R4]. The evidence also suggests that older APOE4 carriers with higher lipid levels may experience accelerated cognitive decline, indicating that apoE-related risk is often intertwined with lipid and metabolic factors [N2-R5]. So, lower APOE levels or risk-associated apoE profiles are consistent with faster cognitive decline, but the association is not uniform and depends on other covariates [N2-F2][N2-R5].

### APOE genotype and protein levels interact with AD diagnosis and progression
APOE genotype and biomarker levels interact in important ways. CSF biomarker studies show that APOE ε4 carriers have reduced CSF Aβ42 and CSF proteins compared with non-carriers, and that APOE genotype correlates with CSF levels of biomarkers during AD progression [N4-F3][N7-R1]. The same study found that the diagnostic performance and critical values of CSF biomarkers differ by genotype [N4-F3]. In addition, higher baseline CSF apoE glycosylation predicted lower rates of increase in CSF t-tau and p-tau181 over 6 years, suggesting that apoE-related biomarker trajectories are dynamic and genotype-dependent [N7-R3]. This means that APOE genotype affects not only biomarker levels but also how those biomarkers are interpreted clinically [N4-F3][N7-R3].

### Human studies on APOE levels, dementia, and biomarker trajectories
Human studies support the broader picture. Plasma apoE levels have been associated with Alzheimer’s disease risk, with low plasma apoE and the presence of the APOE ε4 allele linked to increased AD risk [N4-R3]. CSF biomarker evidence also shows that APOE ε4 carriers had different biomarker levels and biomarker performance across stages of AD, and that longitudinal changes in CSF biomarkers were stronger in APOE ε4 carriers than non-carriers [N4-F3]. The glycosylation study added that higher baseline CSF apoE glycosylation was associated with reduced rates of increase in tau biomarkers, implying that apoE-related changes can track with disease progression [N7-R3]. Overall, the human evidence suggests that lower APOE levels or risk-associated apoE profiles are associated with dementia risk and altered biomarker trajectories, but these associations are best understood as part of a larger genotype-biomarker-clinical cascade [N4-F3][N4-R3][N7-R3].

## 3) Interpretation of APOE levels versus genotype/phenotype distinction

### How APOE genotype, protein levels, and expression differ biologically
APOE genotype sets the main functional class—ε2, ε3, or ε4—but protein levels and expression can vary independently. The evidence shows that plasma levels of apoE and other lipids and lipoproteins are strongly influenced by the APOE polymorphism, and that the ε4 allele is a strong genetic risk factor [N6-R3]. However, knockout and bEKO mouse evidence demonstrate that brain ApoE can be low without plasma ApoE being low, and that plasma lipid levels can independently affect cognition and synaptic function [N5-F4]. This means that low APOE levels are not simply a reflection of genotype; they can also arise from disease processes, lipid dysregulation, or other factors [N5-F4][N6-R3].

### How low levels can be caused by genotype, disease, or other factors
The evidence suggests that low APOE levels may reflect genotype, disease, or other factors. The strongest evidence for genotype is the association between APOE ε4 and increased Alzheimer’s risk, with the ε4 allele linked to reduced CSF Aβ42 and other biomarker changes [N4-F3][N7-R1]. However, the same evidence also shows that low apoE levels can be influenced by glycosylation, lipid changes, and other biomarkers [N4-R4][N7-R3]. In knockout evidence, dyslipidemia and atherosclerosis were separate from ApoE deficiency itself, suggesting that low apoE may sometimes be a secondary effect of broader metabolic or vascular disease [N5-F4]. Therefore, low APOE levels should not be assumed to be equivalent across all individuals or across all contexts [N5-F4][N6-R3].

### How these distinctions affect interpretation of observational and biomarker studies
These distinctions are crucial for interpretation. In biomarker studies, APOE genotype can alter the levels and performance of CSF biomarkers, with critical values depending on genotype [N4-F3]. In observational studies, lower APOE levels may be interpreted as a marker of risk, but they may also be influenced by measurement methods, lipid status, and other covariates [N4-F3][N7-R3]. The evidence therefore supports a nuanced interpretation: APOE genotype is a major risk factor, but it does not fully capture protein levels or expression, and low APOE levels should not be assumed to be equivalent across all individuals or across all contexts [N4-F3][N5-F4][N6-R3]. For biomarker studies, genotype adjustment is needed; for observational studies, confounding and measurement variation remain a concern; and for clinical interpretation, the distinction between genotype, protein levels, and disease state is essential [N4-F3][N5-F4][N6-R3].

## 4) Context for interpretation and limitations of the evidence

### Differences between APOE genotype, protein levels, and expression
The evidence base distinguishes APOE genotype, protein levels, and expression, but the distinction is not always clear-cut. The genotype determines the main functional class, while protein levels and expression can vary independently [N6-R3][N5-F4]. Plasma apoE and other lipids are strongly influenced by the APOE polymorphism, but low APOE levels may also reflect disease or other factors [N6-R3][N5-F4]. This is important because one cannot assume that low levels always mean a specific genotype [N5-F4][N6-R3].

### Study limitations
The evidence repeatedly notes discrepancies in findings across models, cell types, and experimental conditions [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In longitudinal human studies, variability in sample size, age range, follow-up duration, and outcome measures explains mixed results [N2-F2]. The CSF biomarker study explicitly highlights that the performance of biomarkers and critical values differ by APOE genotype, meaning interpretation must be genotype-adjusted [N4-F3]. In biomarker studies, lipid changes, glycosylation, and other factors can also influence outcomes [N4-R4][N7-R3]. These limitations imply that observational and biomarker studies are sensitive to confounding and measurement variation, and that conclusions should be interpreted cautiously [N2-F2][N4-F3].

### How animal models inform human disease but should not be overgeneralized
Animal model evidence is informative but should not be overgeneralized. Knockout mouse studies show synaptic loss and cognitive deficits, but these mice also have dyslipidemia and severe atherosclerosis, which may independently affect brain function [N5-F4]. The bEKO model shows that synaptic loss can persist even when plasma ApoE is normal, but learning deficits were rescued in female bEKO mice, indicating that brain and plasma ApoE are separate parameters [N5-F4]. The review evidence also emphasizes that the role of APOE in preclinical mouse models depends on context [N5-R5]. Therefore, while animal studies provide important mechanistic insights, they must be viewed as hypotheses rather than direct proofs of human disease [N5-F4][N5-R5].

## 5) Integrated synthesis: how low APOE influences cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s pathology

The integrated picture is that low APOE influences AD pathology through multiple interconnected pathways. First, it disrupts Aβ clearance and lipid homeostasis, making the brain less able to manage amyloid-related insults [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Second, it alters microglial activation and neuroinflammation, with ApoE isoforms showing different inflammatory effects and the literature being highly context-dependent [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Third, it worsens synaptic dysfunction and tau pathology, with APOE deficiency inhibiting amyloid-facilitated tau pathology and related neurodegeneration and with APOE3 protecting neurons from Aβ-induced tau damage [N3-R2][N3-R1]. These effects are not isolated; they converge on the same neurodegenerative outcome.

Clinically, lower APOE levels or risk-associated apoE profiles are associated with faster cognitive decline, especially in APOE ε4 carriers, and with altered CSF biomarker levels and trajectories [N2-F2][N4-F3][N7-R3]. However, this association is best understood in the context of genotype, lipid status, and disease state, because low APOE can also be caused by disease, glycosylation, or other factors [N5-F4][N6-R3]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious interpretation: low APOE is a meaningful contributor to AD pathology and cognitive decline, but it is not a simple, universal marker. APOE genotype, protein levels, and expression differ biologically, and observational and biomarker studies must account for those differences when drawing conclusions [N6-R3][N4-F3][N5-F4].

## Bottom line

Low APOE levels influence cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease pathology by interfering with amyloid clearance, lipid homeostasis, microglial activation, and synaptic and tau integrity. The evidence points to a complex, context-dependent biology in which APOE genotype is a major risk factor, but low APOE levels can also reflect disease processes or other factors. In humans, lower APOE levels or risk-associated apoE profiles are associated with faster cognitive decline and altered biomarker trajectories, but interpretation must be genotype-adjusted and cautious about confounding and measurement variation. Animal models provide important mechanistic insights, but they should not be overgeneralized to human disease [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-R2][N5-F4][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R3].
